02992f2b-3701-5bc3-ba32-d5f6226b56ef.name: Bowl (*Sakızlık*)
02992f2b-3701-5bc3-ba32-d5f6226b56ef.short_description: From historical sources, we learn that vessels made of gold and silver were widely used in the Ottoman palace. Starting from the end of the 18th century, Baroque and Rococo forms of Western style replaced classical Ottoman designs. We find roses in relief, the Ottoman coat-of-arms, architectural compositions, casted flowers, birds and animals on a multitude of the vessels of the era. This cylindrical cup with pedestal foot and cupola-like hinged lid was made of vermeil silver. On the body of the cup we see a floral pattern and hanging lambs placed alternatingly. Flowers, buds and leaves are made from rubies and diamonds nailed into gold and silver contours. On the lid – instead of lamb motif on the body – a chalice was used. The foot of the chalice is in the form of a cherub from which a bundle of rays projects.

keywords: minor arts, applied arts, silver objects

05127f0b-387e-53fc-9c38-7c747e046530.name: Reliquary of St. Stephen the King
05127f0b-387e-53fc-9c38-7c747e046530.description:
The reliquary bust of St. Stephen the King, on a base, shows the saint in royal dress. Characteristics of the Baroque style come to the fore in the saint’s head shown in the round and almost imperceptibly turned sideways, with striking features and a soft wavy beard and moustache.  
The bust was probably made by a master craftsman from Rome, influenced by Bernini, while the crown is the work of a contemporary Central European goldsmith.  
The Latin inscription in a cartouche nailed to the front of the base records that Cardinal Francesco Barberini, nephew of Pope Urban VIII, had this bust made in 1635 out of piety for St. Stephen. He commissioned the bust to hold the saint’s skull, endowing the relic with the reverence it deserved. Today it is still in Zagreb Cathedral dedicated to St. Stephen the King.  
St. Stephen, King of Hungary, converted the Hungarians to Christianity and in the early 11th century founded an archbishopric in his hometown Esztergom where he died. He was canonised in 1087 and his cult spread from Hungary to Croatia where it was especially widespread after the Middle Ages. At the time, Hungary and Croatia were in a union and known as the lands of the Crown of St. Stephen after the crown he wore.
05127f0b-387e-53fc-9c38-7c747e046530.short_description: The reliquary of St. Stephen in the form of a bust shows him dressed as a king with a crown on his head. The bust was probably the work of a master craftsman from Rome, influenced by Bernini, while the crown is attributed to a goldsmith from the Central European circle. The Latin inscription in a cartouche on the front of the base verifies that the reliquary was commissioned by Cardinal Barberini in 1635, nephew of Pope Urban VIII, a member of a powerful and wealthy Roman family that died out in the male line in 1736.
05127f0b-387e-53fc-9c38-7c747e046530.method_for_datation:
The 1915 Inventory of Zagreb Cathedral mentions the reliquary.  
A Latin inscription with the year of origin is on a cartouche on the front of the base.
05127f0b-387e-53fc-9c38-7c747e046530.obtention: Cardinal Francesco Barberini gifted the reliquary to Zagreb Cathedral.

0bbaf404-0e91-5630-bcc7-37cb18ebe36e.name: Lion of St. Mark
0bbaf404-0e91-5630-bcc7-37cb18ebe36e.description: The silver lion of St. Mark was a gift from Venice to the council and citizens of the city of Zurich in 1608. At that time, Venice was being besieged by Austria and Spain and sought contact with Protestant cantons; the Venetian ambassador Padavino, who wrote extensively about his trip, was sent to Zurich. His account of the banquet to celebrate the presentation of the lion he had donated contains the report that the lion was circulated in a round of toasts: the head can be removed and used as a tumbler.

0dab6a1c-e333-510c-8838-22f47404def3.name: Chest.
0dab6a1c-e333-510c-8838-22f47404def3.description:
Silver prismatic chest with a lid in the shape of a truncated pyramid. It stands on four moulded rectangular supports that are hollow and smooth. The lid is decorated with two hinges on the rear that have reliefwork depicting birds and flowers, and a third with a medallion-shaped end and two birds facing one another on the front for locking it. The chest is decorated with seeding and with black enamelled scrolls that run around the whole of the piece on the edge of the lid as well as on the top and bottom parts of the chest. In the centre there is an inscription in *kufic* characters, enamelled in the same colour, which translates as: 'Allah's blessing on his people / ever-lasting health … fulfilled / permanent happiness, lasting happiness … wealth … for its owner'. Given that the ironwork interrupts the inscription, we can assume that it was added at a later date. The bevelled sides of the lid bear the following inscription using the same type of enamelled letters, but larger: 'Allah's blessing on the people, / Ever-lasting health and / wealth fulfilled and permanent happiness and …'  
On the upper part of the lid, on a granulated base with black enamelled leaves, there are eight peacocks arranged in three pairs facing each other and two turned towards the sides. The piece does not appear to have been commissioned, but made to sell.  
The kings of León, Fernando I and Doña Sancha, donated it, with other chests, to the collegiate church of San Isidoro de León.
0dab6a1c-e333-510c-8838-22f47404def3.short_description: An unusual Andalusian chest as it is made of silver and decorated with enamel and niello, although it is adorned with inscriptions. Its historical value lies in that it was made in a Taifa kingdom before passing to the king and queen of León, who gave it to the collegiate church of San Isidoro.
0dab6a1c-e333-510c-8838-22f47404def3.dimensions: Height 11 cm, length 17.5 cm, width 11 cm.
0dab6a1c-e333-510c-8838-22f47404def3.method_for_datation: Its formal characteristics date it to the Taifa period. The chest was dedicated by the kings of León, Fernando I and Doña Sancha, to the collegiate church of San Isidoro on 21 December 1063 (13 of Dhu'l-Hijja 455), according to the donation documentation. Its date of manufacture is therefore between the end of the Caliphate of Cordoba (422 / 1031) and the date that it was donated to the collegiate church.
0dab6a1c-e333-510c-8838-22f47404def3.method_for_provenance: As no place of origin is mentioned in the inscription, the chest could have been made in any of the workshops that were dedicated to this kind of activity during the Taifa period. The chest must have come into King Fernando I's possession as war booty or as taxes from one of the Taifas.
0dab6a1c-e333-510c-8838-22f47404def3.provenance: The Taifa from which this piece originates is unknown.
0dab6a1c-e333-510c-8838-22f47404def3.obtention: The chest arrived at the National Archaeological Museum on 20 October 1869 after it was confiscated by the Scientific Commissions that were created after the revolution of 1868.

0dda7d39-b57f-5849-bcea-6897a0d0d4be.name: Amulet
0dda7d39-b57f-5849-bcea-6897a0d0d4be.short_description: Throughout the 19th century in Macedonia, jewellery was not used only for adornment; it also served an apotropaic function. People used to wear various kinds of reliquaries for the purpose of personal protection from evil spirits. These protective items used to be worn in pockets or sewn to the garment. This amulet is made of silver using the techniques of hammering and engraving. The rectangular plate depicts the Virgin and Child flanked by two angels above them. The rings on the sides show that the amulet must have been worn suspended on a chain.

keywords: Reliquary; talisman; metalwork

0ebf3162-8d35-51b9-9c45-05310b813e4a.name: Ewer on a stand
0ebf3162-8d35-51b9-9c45-05310b813e4a.short_description: An ewer with flattened circular sides has a tall tapering neck with a hinged, dome cover and ball finial. A handle is attached below the cover, opposite a small spout. The body rests on a spreading foot. At the center of each side is a rosediamond inset flowerhead surrounded by trefoils within a fine enamelled border of floral cartouches. The associated oval tray features enamelled floral sprays and cartouches on top of four spreading feet terminating in elephant heads.

0f137923-bf0e-59e9-aa6b-2af58599a73c.name: Flint lock pistol
0f137923-bf0e-59e9-aa6b-2af58599a73c.short_description: Following the fall of Seringapatam in 1799 AD, this gun was handed over to Lord Cornwallis (1738–1805 AD), a Governor General and Commander-in-Chief of British army during the third Anglo-Mysorean war (1789–1792 AD) as a trophy. The gun is rich with tiger motifs with complete form of tiger figure on the butt and stylised *bubri* on the barrel as well as inscriptions on different parts of the gun. Images of tigers mauling European soldier on the side plate of the gun represents Tipu’s propaganda in degrading the British East India Company. The gun possessed advanced technology of its time where shooter could fire twice continuously with only a single load.

0f2fd351-f23b-5e56-9d5a-58ba529c43c4.name: Emerald-covered box
0f2fd351-f23b-5e56-9d5a-58ba529c43c4.short_description:
This spectacular gold box has a circular base, vertical sides and a low domed lid. 103 emeralds have been set in the 16 slightly convex rectangular panels of the sides and the 16 curving triangular sections that form the lid. The side panels are carved in shallow relief with cypress trees, their tips curving to the left; the same motif is repeated in the panels on the lid, but the tips of the trees are not curved. Narrow bands of gold frame the emerald panels and a 24-facet diamond is set at the apex of the lid. The base is covered with translucent green enamel and decorated with a central rosette and split acanthus leaves and palmettes.  
Emeralds were mined in Spanish Colombia, exported to Europe and then sent to Ottoman Turkey and Mughal India. Boxes of this type often had a matching tray and they could be used to hold medicines (including opium) or even more precious objects. They are featured in Mughal and Rajput miniature paintings from the end of the 16th century onwards.

0f5d7f4f-d0a8-5393-b615-340244caa48f.name: Water vessel and tobacco bowl support from a *huqqa*
0f5d7f4f-d0a8-5393-b615-340244caa48f.short_description: The water vessel and the tobacco bowl are elements of a water pipe or *huqqa*. Both are decorated with translucent cloisonné and opaque champlevé enamels with flowers, branches of leaves and beautifully dressed and jewelled *peri*s (angels) offering gifts. No other Indian treasury objects with such elaborate enamelled decoration are known. Mark Zebrowski attributed the *huqqa* to an early 18th-century workshop in Mewar, Rajput state.

117e4311-5f29-5b99-9692-18b2ed19cd70.name: Persian sabre
117e4311-5f29-5b99-9692-18b2ed19cd70.short_description: The handle of this sabre is set with ivory, the crossguard with large sapphires and emeralds; the blade is decorated with gilt engraved etchings that contain the year AD 1813 and the name of Fath Ali (AD 1797–1834), the then reigning Shah. Following a long and costly war with Russia, the Shah signed the Peace of Golestan in AD 1813. Perhaps the sword was presented to Emperor Franz I of Austria (AD 1768–1835) that year in an attempt to build a new alliance with Austria as a counterweight to Russia.

1557e889-e4c0-511e-92f2-cf332ab357cf.name: Incense burner.
1557e889-e4c0-511e-92f2-cf332ab357cf.description: A circular incense burner with a hinged domed cover, standing on three curved feet in the form of stylised horse hooves. The cover is pierced to emit smoke. Christian figures with haloes, some carrying Christian liturgical items that include a cross and censer, inhabit the lobed arches around the body and cover; all but one is facing in a clockwise direction. Both the male and the female figures wear a long-sleeved gown which reaches almost to the ankles, with a shawl draped over the right shoulder. All the figures are bare-headed except for the one holding a cross who wears a turban. The medallion that does not contain a figure and which stands between two inhabited arches, was probably once the place of a handle. There is a benedictory inscription in kufic script around the apex of the lid to an anonymous owner. This burner belongs to a group of metal objects with Christian figures made during the Ayyubid period that may have been intended for either Muslim or Christian patrons. Given the fine quality of this burner it was evidently not a mass-produced household object but was more likely to have been created for a wealthy patron. The shape of the burner stems from the Byzantine tradition which continued to be popular in both Egypt and Syria during the 13th and 14th centuries.
1557e889-e4c0-511e-92f2-cf332ab357cf.short_description: This incense burner is one of a group of inlaid metal objects with Christian figures made in Syrian or Mesopotamian workshops. It could have been commissioned for either a Muslim or a Christian patron.
1557e889-e4c0-511e-92f2-cf332ab357cf.type: Metalwork, decoration object, silver and gold
1557e889-e4c0-511e-92f2-cf332ab357cf.dimensions: Height 20 cm, width 12.5 cm, depth 12.5 cm.
1557e889-e4c0-511e-92f2-cf332ab357cf.method_for_datation: Both the technique and decoration resemble several metal objects produced in Mosul and Syria in the 13th century, including objects such as the Blacas Ewer made in Mosul in 1232 (now in the British Museum), or a candlestick made in Syria in 1248–9, (now in the Musée des Arts décoratifs in Paris).
1557e889-e4c0-511e-92f2-cf332ab357cf.method_for_provenance: The technique and decoration on this burner can be compared to that of other metal objects produced in Mosul and cities in Syria in the 13th century. The similarity of technique and style between the metalwork of northern Mesopotamia and Syria is due to the movement of metalworkers from Mosul to Syria in search of work under the Ayyubid sultans. For example, a ewer in the Louvre in Paris (dated AH 657 / AD 1258) was made by Husain Ibn Muhammad of Mosul for the Ayyubid Sultan Salah al-Din Yusuf, who ruled from Damascus.

178f74aa-fe42-524b-94f2-f5d4a1c1bd50.name: Processional Altar of St. John the Evangelist
178f74aa-fe42-524b-94f2-f5d4a1c1bd50.description:
A silver processional altar made at the beginning of the 18th century, which belonged to the Royal Monastery of Our Lady of Conception, and was used in the Procession of the Holy Sacrament in Beja. The social and religious significance of the Corpus Christi Day procession cannot be understated; it represents one of the greatest manifestations of the Portuguese Baroque, which once acknowledged, justifies the sumptuousness of some of the pieces used in these ceremonies. Traditionally, up until 1893, the altar was carried by farmers.  
Rectangular in shape, the *acroteria* (small bases placed at the four extremities) has a beaded edging, and four *albarradas* or ornamental vases, alternate with smaller jars in the middle. The entirety is covered with vegetable and scalloped-shell ornamentation, and St. James' crosses. The wooden carrying rods are also silver plated.  
The octagonal shaped pedestal stands over the main body, decorated with double scalloped-shell ornamentation, pear-shaped “tables” and St. James' crosses. There is also an octagonal platform with small jars placed at each corner of the pedestal.  
An iron column rises above the pedestal, covered with silk cloth embroidered with gold thread. It meets a gold and silver halo embellished with precious stones above which a gold and silver crown rests, also studded with precious stones. In the middle of the altarpiece, the Martyrdom of St. John the Evangelist is played out, the saint graphically shown immersed in boiling olive oil. The wooden effigy of the saint with clasped hands looks straight up at the sky. The silver boiler, standing on a silver tripod above the fire, is kept alight by two multicoloured wooden figures, kneeling at either side of the boiler. One of them is blowing and the other is using a solid-silver pitchfork.  
The patrons of the altarpiece were a group of nuns devoted to St. John the Evangelist. There was another group of nuns in the same convent that devoted themselves to St. John the Baptist and commissioned a similar processional altar in honour of the saint. In fact, both altarpieces date from the beginning of the 18th century and were made in the same workshop. They both show the same crowned stamps of the city of Lisbon and the same maker's letter “M”.
178f74aa-fe42-524b-94f2-f5d4a1c1bd50.short_description: A silver processional altar made at the beginning of the 18th century, it portrays features typical of the Portuguese Baroque at the time of King João V. Designed to represent the Martyrdom of St. John the Evangelist, the piece belonged to the Royal Monastery of Our Lady of Conception and was used in the procession of the Holy Sacrament in Beja, on Corpus Christi Day.

18e02623-b9ad-5163-8ba9-d958a15a6f01.short_description: Wooden handled dagger with thin silver sheath; incurved geometric designs on the obverse side; inset with turquoise and black stones. The dagger was used by both Bedouins and villagers as part of men’s traditional garb. This object reflects the diverse population composition of Jordan in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It also demonstrates personal attire, fashion, local costumes and rites.

2363b57a-3e83-58d6-add7-b8e17a845595.name: Belt elements
2363b57a-3e83-58d6-add7-b8e17a845595.short_description: Composed of a central rosette, eight bars and two finials, these belt elements are decorated with domes and granulation designs. Several features compare with Iranian pieces including the box construction and the minute granulation covering completely most of the domes. An early date is supported by the conspicuous absence of openwork filigree used in Fatimid jewellery. Similar belt elements were found in the Bekaa valley in Lebanon, in a hoard of Mamluk and other later jewellery.

25a5389e-c95f-5ff4-9837-134e5233173f.short_description: This exquisite perfume bottle is designed as a gem-set fish, entirely decorated with uncut rubies, emeralds, turquoise and pearls. The tip of the small bottle opens with a screw cap. It was most probably meant to contain perfume or a powder for cosmetic use. Jewelled objects from the Mughal period, such as this bottle, were commissioned for the courtly elite and would probably have been worn attached to a belt or around the neck.

2820044b-9046-518a-901e-821f3cb8b715.name: Arabian gold dagger
2820044b-9046-518a-901e-821f3cb8b715.short_description: Arabian (Omani) dagger belonging to Sheikh Abdullah bin Jassim. The dagger sheath is made of leather and embroidered with golden thread. 2b9bd4b7-9bf4-5be0-b693-18e62b5dc6f7.name: Drinking cup
2b9bd4b7-9bf4-5be0-b693-18e62b5dc6f7.short_description: Small silver cup with a stepped pedestal for drinking hard liquors. The surface is decorated with geometric designs, including dots, lines and triangles. On the upper part of the cup, an engraved inscription in Russian ("your health") runs along the external surface. The year of manufacture (1896) is stamped. Items like this were brought to Jordan in the last quarter of the 19th century by Caucasian immigrants, the Circassians. The immigration of the Circassians started in the middle of nineteenth century and continued until 1900. They migrated to the eastern Arab countries with which they have spiritual and religious links. This object illustrates the variegated population composition of Jordan in the late 19th and early 20th centuries and the various local costumes, crafts and rites.

The walls are adorned with vertically disposed, wavy bands, every second one further enhanced by leafy stalks. These bowls were made in Southern Hungary and the Balkans and used for personal, ritual and religious occasions.

3014d292-46d6-5552-8846-8782d58e0b90.name: Foot reliquary
3014d292-46d6-5552-8846-8782d58e0b90.description: When Basel split into two half-cantons in 1833, the famous Basel Minster Treasure suffered the same fate. The new Canton Basel-Landschaft received 64 per cent of the treasure, but because it was desperately short of funds, it converted the ecclesiastical riches into cash, among them the silver reliquary of 1450, which brought the exchequer 562 francs. The reliquary has the shape of a foot, consistent with its contents – allegedly the foot bones of a young boy who was murdered in Bethlehem on Herod’s command. What chills modern viewers to the bone today, used to be the object of religious devotion to many. Through a of rock glass opening believers could catch a glimpse of the sacred relic and hope for divine assistance.

3029fa98-e9e3-5645-84dd-415d0952a243.name: Water pipe (*ghalian*)
3029fa98-e9e3-5645-84dd-415d0952a243.short_description: Tobacco was introduced into the Islamic world from the American colonies and, together with coffee and tea, became a popular form of social refreshment. In Iran, elaborate water pipes such as this one were made of precious materials and enamelled in several colours to heighten the pleasure derived from smoking. Tobacco was placed in the bowl of the water pipe and water into the base to cool the smoke prior to inhalation.

32629ea7-5978-5c34-ac5e-6fa3012db355.name: Reliquary Chest of St. João de Brito
32629ea7-5978-5c34-ac5e-6fa3012db355.description:
The Portuguese established trading posts along the coasts of India and China where merchants could trade and store their merchandise, extending their authority into the hinterland. While the traditional political structures of local chieftains remained, the elite profited by reselling European wares. In addition to trade, the Portuguese sought to spread Christianity among the local Asian populations with Franciscan, Dominican and later Jesuit missionaries preaching to the indigenous peoples. The Christian missionaries learned the native languages, familiarised themselves with the indigenous cultures and even their religions; in this effort, the Jesuits were extremely dedicated. St. João de Brito was sent as a member of the Jesuit Order to the mission of Maduré, in India, in 1673. His aim was to convert the higher castes, in order to better establish Christianity in the region. He became a *pandaraswami*, an Indian ascetic. One of his converts, Prince Tadaya Theva upon becoming Christian, was rejected by one of his wives. She complained to her uncle, the Raja of Marava, who had the Jesuit executed in Orbyur, India, in 1690.  
This chest, with a pyramidal lid engraved in low-relief, features scenes of St. João de Brito's life and martyrdom. The bas-relief on the top features the saint in Indian dress, with sandals and a staff. Several winged cherubs in chiselled silver flank the lid. The body of the chest presents two sculpted winged angels on each side in true Baroque expression. Four elaborate feet in gilded silver hold the main body. Commissioned by King Pedro II of Portugal as a royal homage to the Jesuit saint, the Portuguese coat of arms is seen in the centre testifying to the royal provenance.  
The presence of the *Agnus Dei* on the top may have been a later addition by the Jesuits, who used it on special occasions as a Eucharistic tabernacle for the veneration of the Blessed Sacrament.

39b49b4c-4d71-5eb2-ae22-21ea92dca300.name: Box with the image of an artillery emplacement of the Austro-Hungarian Army at the Sinai in 1916
39b49b4c-4d71-5eb2-ae22-21ea92dca300.short_description: This silver box was made in memory of the Sinai Desert campaign embarked upon by soldiers of the Austro-Hungarian Army. At the end of 1915, two Austro-Hungarian artillery units were transported to reach the front at Gallipoli after a demand for support from the Ottoman Empire. In 1916, the 15cm howitzer battery was transferred to Smyrna and the mobile 24cm mortar battery was stationed near Haifa in Palestine to defend Mount Carmel. Other parts of the unit took part in the battle of Gaza and remained in the area till 1918. The last members of these Austro-Hungarian units were finally repatriated to Trieste in 1919.

3a110f14-cb1d-5cf4-bcbf-686eae047043.name: Horse bridle.
3a110f14-cb1d-5cf4-bcbf-686eae047043.description:
A part of a bridle or halter that would have been placed around a horse’s head; made of gold and enamel sections through which leather straps pass. These small oblong-shaped sections are decorated with gold filigree alternating with blue, red, white and green cloisonné enamel. The enamel compartments are filled with arabesques in opaque red and white against a background of translucent green and blue. The style and decorative techniques belong to a long tradition in Islamic Spain. However, the design of this bridle relates to Nasrid architecture, in particular certain stucco panels in the Alhambra Palace in Granada. Therefore this piece was certainly made in Granada but not necessarily for a Muslim patron.  
The decoration on this bridle can be connected to that seen on a hilt and scabbard (in the Museo del Ejercito), and a scabbard and mounts of a dagger (in the Real Armería). Previously in the collection of the Vieana Family, it has been suggested that after the battle of Lucana in AH 887/ AD 1483, one of the ancestors of this family took these pieces of armoury, which had belonged to Abu Abd Allah Muhammad XI (or Boabdil) the last sultan of the Nasrid dynasty of Granada (r. AH 886–96 / AD 1482–92).
3a110f14-cb1d-5cf4-bcbf-686eae047043.short_description: It is uncertain exactly where and when this luxury horse bridle was made. Gold and enamel decoration belonged to a long tradition known in many parts of Islamic Spain, however, it was probably made for the Nasrid court as the design recalls certain stucco panels in the Alhambra Palace in Granada.
3a110f14-cb1d-5cf4-bcbf-686eae047043.dates: Hegira late 9th–early 10th century / AD late 15th–early 16th century.
3a110f14-cb1d-5cf4-bcbf-686eae047043.method_for_datation:
This bridle is close in design to a group of objects associated with Abu Abd Allah Muhammad XI (or Boabdil), the last sultan of the Nasrid dynasty of Granada (r. 886–96 / 1482–92).  
Although it is not certain that it was made for this ruler, the technique and design fit with other gold and enamel work produced in the late 9th / 15th century.
3a110f14-cb1d-5cf4-bcbf-686eae047043.method_for_provenance: The enamel and gold filigree on this bridle recall stucco designs in the Alhambra Palace, Granada, Spain.

3b20eedf-73ef-58bb-867b-4bd1624b5b9c.name: Silver service.
3b20eedf-73ef-58bb-867b-4bd1624b5b9c.description:
A silver service consisting of identical pairs of candlesticks, incense burners and perfume sprinklers. 'Adila, the daughter of Sultan Mahmud II, presented the service as a gift to al-Aqsa Mosque. The design is heavily influenced by the European style.  
Each of the candlesticks is composed of a base, a shaft, a body, neck and the candleholder. The base of the candlestick is broad and octagonal in form, and is adorned with engraved leaf decorations. The base is connected to the body via the shaft, on top of which is a cupped ledge in the form of a leaf. The leaf-shaped ledge curves upwards, resembling the leaves engraved on the base. The body of the candlestick is composed of two globular areas: the lower one resembles a small sphere, while the one above it is a relatively large ovoid. Both are decorated with leafy engraved motifs similar to those that decorate the base. The body is connected to the neck, where there is another cupped leaf-shaped ledge, resembling that below it and of approximately the same size.  
Both the incense burners and the perfume sprinklers resemble each other, for each piece is composed of a base, body and punctured neck; the base fluted and wide, narrowing immediately. The base of one of the incense burners carries an Ottoman inscription in Arabic letters that reads: “Sultan Mahmud Han Sani hazretlerinin kerimesi, devletlü, ismetlü Adile Sultan hazretlerinin Mescid-i Aksa'ya mahsus vakfıdır.” (“Endowment of her Excellency Adile Sultan, daughter of his Excellency Sultan Mahmud Han II, to al-Aqsa Mosque.”)  
The date “1305” \[AD 1887\] is inscribed on it as well. This date was added during the reign of the Ottoman sultan, 'Abd al-Hamid II (r. AH 1293–1327 / AD 1876–1909). The body of the incenser is globular and fluted in form, slender at the bottom in order to adhere to the base, and at the top in order to cleave to the neck. The middle of the body is divided into two: the upper and the lower parts, which are connected to each other by a hinge, whereby one can open the censer and fill it. The necks of the incense burners are punctured to permit the fragrance to escape, similarly the necks of the sprinklers terminate with holes from which to sprinkle perfume and, like the incensers, they open at the apex in order to fill the inside of the sprinkler with perfume. Both the incense burners and perfume sprinklers end with a small globular section decorated with vegetal leaves, which resemble those decorating the candlesticks.

3e0c77fe-e569-53cb-a6e6-0d26f3ac626b.name: Coffee pot
3e0c77fe-e569-53cb-a6e6-0d26f3ac626b.short_description:
This copper pot has been covered in a thin layer of silver and lavishly decorated. Its swelling shape shows the influence of the European Baroque style on the Ottoman decorative arts. Most metal coffee pots were made of cheaper materials such as tinned copper. In richer homes, coffee was served to honoured guests in pots like this one, made of precious metals (or imitations of them) and decorated in the latest taste.  
The Ottoman Baroque style developed from the 1740s as artists and designers began to apply non-figurative European motifs to Ottoman forms. It flourished until the 1820s, when new types of European ornament were introduced.

keywords: coffee; metalwork; Ottoman Baroque

4b991957-3850-5dff-ab19-d438bef7536d.name: Pre-Islamic ewer with female figures
4b991957-3850-5dff-ab19-d438bef7536d.short_description:
This silver-gilt ewer was made in Pre-Islamic times during the Sassanid dynasty. Four dancing female figures are depicted on the vessel’s pear-shaped body, each holding a ceremonial object. The women are framed by embossed arches and accompanied by birds. The neck of the vessel is decorated with a vine-leaf pattern.  
The iconography of dancing female figures is often associated with the maenads, attendants of the god Dionysus in Greek mythology. As the vessel is from the Sassanid dynasty, the link to Greek mythology is uncertain. It has been suggested that the motif of dancing figures originated in the Iranian cult of the goddess Anahita, where the ewer could have been used to serve wine during court celebrations or religious ceremonies. There is no evidence, however, to support this hypothesis.

4e0e7286-5def-51f5-b4c3-162106c6828c.name: Silverware used on the Orient Express
4e0e7286-5def-51f5-b4c3-162106c6828c.short_description: After the Crimean War, Ottoman authorities concluded that a railway connecting Europe with Istanbul was necessary. The construction of a new terminal building began on 11 February 1888. The terminal building is one of the most famous examples of European Orientalism, and has influenced the designs of other architects. The Orient Express was the name of a long-distance passenger train service originally operated by the *Compagnie Internationale des Wagons-Lits*. The route passed through Strasbourg, Karlsruhe, Stuttgart, Ulm, and Munich in Germany, Vienna in Austria, Budapest in Hungary, Bucharest in Romania, Rousse and Varna in Bulgaria and ending in Sirkeci.

4f197f6e-373b-5299-bc3c-8c7b6db1240e.name: Pair of pistols, a diplomatic present of Sidi Mohammed II, Bey (1855–1859) of Tunis, to Emperor Franz Joseph
4f197f6e-373b-5299-bc3c-8c7b6db1240e.short_description: This pair of flintlock pistols was ordered by the Bey of Tunis from the French gunsmith Claude Bizouard, who worked in Marseille. 518efda2-0584-5f56-8e0c-1de2b1a46456.name: Silver rosewater sprinkler
518efda2-0584-5f56-8e0c-1de2b1a46456.short_description: This solid silver rosewater sprinkler forms part of a set. Its body is made from several sections, including the foot, the body, the three sections making up the neck and the sprinkler finial. Its relief decoration reflects a fusion of Asian, Islamic and Western traditions, the lotus shape of its body symbolizing purity and spiritual light.

51e979e1-5041-52d1-b9e1-0d200f1af77f.name: Monstrance from Kopřivná
51e979e1-5041-52d1-b9e1-0d200f1af77f.description:
The pedestal of this monstrance, with its relief and shell-like ornamentation, is decorated with angels’ heads, their eyes turned to heaven. The stem is a simply rendered figure of the Virgin Mary standing on a crescent moon and globe, encircled by a serpent. The spiral kinesis is enhanced by the modelling of clouds, corn stalks and grapes on a casket crowned with the figure of God the Father and an angel adoring a cross decorated with red glass.  
The uniquely shaped monstrance with the Virgin Mary Immaculata was designed by Franz Ignaz Günther as part of his decoration of the Church of the Holy Trinity in Kopřivná. The church was built by Jan Ludvík of Žerotín-Lilgenau on the border between north Moravia and Silesia as a memorial pilgrimage site. The monstrance was made to fit the high altar tabernacle, below Günther’s statue of the Immaculata.  
The composition drew on Günther’s design of a copper monstrance for Munich, as well as on Egid Quirin Asam’s design of a monstrance for the Church of St. John of Nepomuk, also in Munich. All of these were preceded by a diamond monstrance in the Loretto, Prague, which was made in Vienna and designed by Johann Bernard Fischer of Erlach.  
The silversmith who executed the design participated in the creation of the Holy Trinity Column, Olomouc and the tomb of Olomouc Bishop Schrattenbach (Kroměříž, Church of St. Mauritz). Günther arrived in Olomouc after journeyman service in Augsburg, Nuremberg, Frankfurt, Linz and Vienna and worked for the Count of Žerotín. In 1757 he studied at the Vienna Academy in Munich, where he settled, becoming one of the most influential Bavarian sculptors of the 18th century.  
During the Baroque period, the monstrance became a decorative object worthy of adoration, apart from its practical use of carrying the Holy Communion.
51e979e1-5041-52d1-b9e1-0d200f1af77f.short_description: A uniquely shaped monstrance with the Virgin Mary Immaculata it was created in an Olomouc metal workshop to the design of later famous Munich sculptor, Franz Ignaz Günther. It was part of his overall decoration for the Church of the Holy Trinity in Kopřivná, on the border between north Moravia and Silesia.

521d6cfc-68ec-53af-a60c-48b720b5bbf7.name: Armchairs
521d6cfc-68ec-53af-a60c-48b720b5bbf7.short_description: The armchairs are veneered with ivory, engraved with flowers and leaves as well as mythical beasts and birds. Featuring a central mirror framed with studded tortoiseshell above various openwork rails, the back embellished with metal jewel-like cartouches. The seat on flutes solid ivory front legs and swept forward back legs are supported by engraved gilt brass and gold peacocks with mechanical springs that make the wings flap when weight is applied to their backs. The association of peacocks with thrones, however, goes back to Shah Jahan's famous peacock throne, built in AD 1635.

531f2f47-2ae4-509e-a2e9-99d2a1ea93da.name: Ornament from a Janissary’s cap
531f2f47-2ae4-509e-a2e9-99d2a1ea93da.short_description: The military supremacy that had helped make the Ottomans a world power was largely based on the highly disciplined Janissary corps – crack infantry troops. As a part of their uniform, the Janissaries wore a distinctive felt hat somewhat like a stocking cap in appearance, known as a *börk*, to which was affixed just above the forehead an ornament such as this rare silver gilt example. The slightly concave device, decorated with delicately worked geometric designs, would have held an insignia demonstrating the Janissary's loyalty to the Sultan–possibly a feather or even a spoon, signifying that it was the ruler who provided him with his daily soup.
531f2f47-2ae4-509e-a2e9-99d2a1ea93da.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
531f2f47-2ae4-509e-a2e9-99d2a1ea93da.method_for_datation: The decoration of this object, including eight- and six-pointed stars against a scrolling background, is identical to janissary hat ornaments captured from the Ottomans after the Battle of Vienna in 1683, establishing a probable terminus ante quem (e.g., Museum of Karlsruhe, Baden Germany).
531f2f47-2ae4-509e-a2e9-99d2a1ea93da.method_for_provenance: The same type of ornament is represented attached to the distinctive Ottoman military hat in paintings, lithographs and photographs of Ottoman janissaries; the hat with ornament carved in stone forms the upper part of janissary tombstones, while a few actual hats have survived with their ornaments (e.g., Museum of Karlsruhe, Baden, Germany).

53b64031-daec-570d-8bd3-6cd325cad7a9.name: Dagger (Tams Type)
53b64031-daec-570d-8bd3-6cd325cad7a9.short_description: This dagger provides an excellent example of the Arabesque in Islamic design. The term, "Arabesque", can be defined in two ways; as a specific decorative element consisting of a continuous branching stem with split palmate leaves, or in a larger sense, used to refer to an entire range of designs based on stylised floral, foliar and animal motifs. The aesthetics of the Arabesque are derived from the imposition of order on the natural world. Arabesque patterns are used extensively in traditional Omani woodwork, plasterwork and metalwork as a means of covering entire surfaces or precise areas within a defined geometric framework.

keywords: Arabesque; Dagger; Metalwork
materials: Ivory, wood, gold threads, silver, steel

5cf8b622-bc23-5c90-a393-46a79bb0514b.name: Reliquary of St-George Chiopolites from Aivali
5cf8b622-bc23-5c90-a393-46a79bb0514b.short_description: The reliquary contained the head of George Chiopolites, who was martyred in Aïvali / Kydonies in 1807. The container made for the head has intricate rococo decoration with ribbons, bows, roses, blank heraldic shields and St George holding the attributes of a neomartyr under the imposing two-headed eagle of ecclesiastical authority. From the mid-eighteenth century, thanks to special administrative treatment or privileges, the inhabitants of Aïvali transformed what had been a small fishing village into a flourishing commercial centre on the Aeolian coast. The inscription on the reliquary refers to the goldsmith and to the Guild of Soap-Makers, which was one of the biggest trade associations in the town. It also refers to Sophronios, who oversaw the commissioning, and has been identified to the parish priest and a close relative of Theophilos Kaïris, a teacher at the Academy of Kydonies who was later expelled from the Church under the free Greek state for his revolutionary ideas and was to die in prison, the last ideologue of the Enlightenment.

keywords: relic; rococo

63495f88-3241-51a5-a473-0ac5b48f3bde.name: Septum Nose Ring
63495f88-3241-51a5-a473-0ac5b48f3bde.short_description:
This is a nose ring worn through the nasal septum. Such nose rings serve as a marker of ethnic identity and marital status among elderly Arab women in and around the city of Bukhara. The nose ring is made of silver wire and can be opened by unfastening the upper section from a loop on the lower section. The lower section is decorated with a beige semi-precious stone marked by brown veining. This stone is flanked by two cuboid beads made of soldered silver spheres, and then by two spiral-shaped beads made of silver wire. A thin silver wire forms the middle section. Each of its ends is twisted around the base of the ring, just above each of the the spiral-shaped beads. This middle section is decorated with a river pearl, two round beads made of soldered silver spheres, and a pair of asymmetrical coral beads.  
In the 20th century, the tradition of wearing septum nose rings became obsolete in Central Asia, with the exception of Arabic regions. Nose rings were altered into earrings (as in the case of this artefact). Bukhara nose rings are distinguished by the presence of decoration on two separate sections of the lower portion, one above the other.

6683cc1c-52e6-5a4a-a227-4855d653487b.name: Rosewater bottle.
6683cc1c-52e6-5a4a-a227-4855d653487b.description:
The rosewater bottle has a pear-shaped body and a short round base. The tall, slender neck is shaped like a cypress tree and is fitted to the body with a knob, which has vegetal decoration and turns on a shaft.  
  
Pieces of polished turquoise are attached to the body, a technique called *firuzekari*. An openwork design with alternating bunches of tulips, roses and carnations, and cypress trees, has been created by carving out the metal background. There are *firuzekari* cypress trees on the sprinkler as well as palmettes in the same technique on the base. The entire surface is decorated with rubies and emeralds fitted into sockets. *Firuzekari* and gold were used decoratively on Qur'an covers in particular, during the last quarter of the AH 10th century / AD 16th century.  
  
Turquoise, a greenish-blue gemstone, is considered in Turkish popular culture to this day to be a talisman against the evil eye and is thought to prevent bad luck and accidents.  
  
In the Ottoman period such rosewater bottles, exquisitely crafted and decorated with precious stones, were used mostly by palace officials. Rosewater bottles were made of gold, silver, porcelain and glass; they had long necks, narrow mouths and large bodies. They were used for pouring or sprinkling rosewater over the hands of guests, including at religious gatherings such as *mevlid* (the celebration of the birthday of the Prophet). Normally a rosewater bottle would also have a tray and be used together with an incense-burner during such ceremonies.
6683cc1c-52e6-5a4a-a227-4855d653487b.short_description: Rosewater was sprinkled on guests' hands during religious ceremonies and private meetings. Gold rosewater bottles were especially used by courtiers. According to Islamic tradition, rosewater carries the fragrance of 'rose', the symbol of Prophet Muhammad and its use adds to the meaning of the worship.
6683cc1c-52e6-5a4a-a227-4855d653487b.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
6683cc1c-52e6-5a4a-a227-4855d653487b.dates: Hegira last quarter of the 10th century / AD 16th century.
6683cc1c-52e6-5a4a-a227-4855d653487b.method_for_datation: Naturalistic motifs of tulips, roses, hyacinths, cypresses and pomegranates started to infuse the Ottoman decorative repertory in about the middle of the 10th / 16th century. As such motifs are found on our example as well as on similar works of art at the Topkapı Palace Treasury, this rosewater bottle is dated to the last quarter of the 10th / 16th century.
6683cc1c-52e6-5a4a-a227-4855d653487b.method_for_provenance: The high-quality workmanship, as well as the existence of similar objects at the Topkapı Palace, suggests that this bottle was made in the Topkapı Palace workshops in Istanbul.

6a6e9eb9-6672-5c93-a85f-f911188ec1ce.name: Tankard
6a6e9eb9-6672-5c93-a85f-f911188ec1ce.description: This tankard follows the pattern of Persian jugs of the 15th century. Its rich figurative decoration is reminiscent of the decorative strips used in book painting. The decor gives this tankard a special position in the context of Ottoman silver works, which in most cases present ornamental decoration only.

6b91356f-d7c7-598c-9081-59fee1195ec8.name: *Ghulamiyyah* (Ear Ornaments)
6b91356f-d7c7-598c-9081-59fee1195ec8.short_description:
A traditional affinity for symmetry and balance is manifested in the use of strong geometric forms across the entire range of Omani craft categories. An underlying structure of spheres and hemispheres, cylinders, pyramids, cones, cubes and prisms is the basis for pottery production, metalwork, woven palm work, carpentry and architecture.  
  
The fundamental strength of cylindrical and spherical forms lends structural integrity to a wide variety of forms, such as thrown and coiled pots and the towers, pillars and domes of monumental buildings, as well as influencing the design of these earrings.

6ba08a0e-aff8-5310-8058-e535621f5827.name: Bookcover
6ba08a0e-aff8-5310-8058-e535621f5827.short_description: The exterior cover of this binding is made from brown leather with gilded motif. The main panel of the binding is decorated with scalloped almond-shaped medallion with two pendants decorated with arabesque and *hatayi* motifs, and cloud scrolls. Four angulated corner-pieces demarcate the panel with similar decorations. A finely gilded border with S-shaped motif edge the binding. The fore-edge flap is decorated with four cartouches painted in gold lines with small floral decoration. Part of the decoration on the binding is repeated on the flap with a smaller medallion sits at the apex. The inner part of the binding is decorated in simple designs, yet retain the feel of the centre and corner-piece concept. An obloid-shaped medallion, a variant, adorns the centre of the inner cover with a set of pendants. The medallion, with scalloped edge, is filled with gold dust, as so the pendants. Edging the binding is similar motif as found on the outer cover. The same goes to the decorative piece on the inner part of the flap, which has a small scalloped almond-shaped medallion at the meeting point filled with gold dust. Contacts between dynasties were known to affect artistic developments. Turkish bindings followed the Persian decorative theme; central medallion, corner-pieces and a decorated border until the 17th century. Nevertheless, the artists created their own particular and combination motifs identifiable as Turkish.

72d19579-3fb8-5a79-846a-370310122503.name: Necklace Inscribed with the *Ayat al-Kursi*
72d19579-3fb8-5a79-846a-370310122503.short_description:
The *ayat al-Kursi* (Throne Verse) is one of the most widely used inscriptions in Oman jewellery. Comprising the 225th verse of the second half of the Noble Quran, is provides an emphatic description of God's power over the universe. Usually referred to as "The Verse of the Throne", in translation it reads:  
'Allah, There is no God but Him, the Living, the External One. Neither slumber nor sleep overtakes  
Him. He is what the Heavens and the earth contains. Who can intercede with Him except by His permission? He knows what is beyond and behind men. They can grasp only that part of His  
knowledge which He wills. His throne is as vast as heavens and the earth, and the preservation of  
both doesn't weary Him. He is the Exalted, the Immense One.

7836bfad-c498-589a-9b61-d970c0703dbb.name: Small bottle for kohl (*m’kihla*).
7836bfad-c498-589a-9b61-d970c0703dbb.description:
This *m'kihla* consists of a convex base that supports the body, which is in the shape of a vase and which features a floral decoration in the baroque Ottoman style. This vase, endowed with two handles in the form of foliage, can be closed with a lid, which is surmounted by a bird, whose tail is linked to the handles via a small chain.  
The two sides of the body, the lid and one of the handles are hallmarked.  
This small bottle is used to keep kohl, or antimony sulphide powder, which was used by women to darken the rims of their eyelids with the aid of a *merwed* (stalk).
7836bfad-c498-589a-9b61-d970c0703dbb.short_description: This kohl flask consists of a concave base bearing an Ottoman baroque-style vase decorated with floral motifs and stamping, fitted with two foliage-shaped handles. It is closed with a lid crowned by a bird from whose tail hangs a chain that is connected to the handles.

7a94e504-793e-5d4f-8a12-0fe92e32a0e7.name: Jug with depiction of animals
7a94e504-793e-5d4f-8a12-0fe92e32a0e7.short_description: The shape of this jug with handles ending in dragon heads comes from Timurid Iran. On the body of the jug and amidst Ottoman decoration hunting scenes are depicted with fantastic and real animals. On the neck paradisiac scenes: two naked figures under a tree, a bear holding a musical instrument and peaceful animals. This animal style originates in German Renaissance silver and was adapted into the repertory of the Balkan Christian workshops before passing into the Iznik ceramics.

7c5b0aa9-383a-5b52-bc5a-91c986d3c9eb.name: Toiletries
7c5b0aa9-383a-5b52-bc5a-91c986d3c9eb.short_description: In the 19th century the wealthy families of Tunis invented the notion of the knastrou l'aroussa (marriage basket) as a mark of their wealth. Made of engraved or watermarked silver, this basket would contain various toiletries for the bride: a perfume sprinkler (mrach), a khol phial with applicator for the eyes (mokhala), a round or rectangular-framed mirror with engraved floral motifs, and a knife and plate for henna. A pair of clogs (qobqabs) made of wood and covered in silver worn by the bride. As a traditional bath (hammam) was the bride's first event on her wedding day, all her toiletries were set out ready for her, with a series of tools for exfoliation, depilation, application of a clay face mask, and more.

7fd24a74-b039-5ba4-b6a9-6fe4522c585f.name: Gold necklace.
7fd24a74-b039-5ba4-b6a9-6fe4522c585f.description:
A gold necklace decorated with exquisitely interwoven ornamentation, which assumes the form of intertwined vegetal boughs. The necklace is composed of two chains joined to 20 *sumluks* (an oval shaped ornamental unit), which are decorated with interwoven vegetal tendrils. Tiny blossoms are suspended from 16 *sumluks,* each of which ends in a pearl-drop. A pendant in the shape of an inverted crescent hangs down from the two central *sumluks*; the pendant is stamped with an inscription written in *naskhi* script and coloured enamel, which reads: 'Eternal Glory'. A circular medallion with a large carnelian lobe in its centre is suspended from the pendant. On the left and right of the pendant, are two other pendants (suspended from two *sumluks)*, the centres of which are adorned by a lobe from the 'bloodstone' – a type of carnelian agate.  
Muslim craftsman used a number of techniques to decorate jewellery, including inlay with precious gems and enamel, high- and low-relief carving, filigree, latticework and incising. In the decoration of this piece, the art of interweaving or latticework was used, which involved the preparation of gold to form long wires that were then shaped into decorative intertwining forms connected together by specialised welding.

80a20f33-dec8-5441-9c8c-72503f119db0.name: Tall ewer
80a20f33-dec8-5441-9c8c-72503f119db0.short_description: The ewer has an ovoid body with a high pedestal foot and a pointed flat pouring spout. It does not retain its handle. The body is decorated with three oval medallions, the two on either side with a winged lion or a gryphon facing forward with a raised forepaw and a forked tongue, while the central one is decorated with a double-headed eagle. The space in between the medallions is filled with trefoil palmettes. The neck and the foot are enriched with a band of roundels containing quatrefoils. Achaemenid and Roman influences are notable respectively in the winged lion as a motif and in the niello decoration of the neck and foot. These elements demonstrate the multicultural influences on later Sasanian metalwork. However, a dating towards the beginning of the Islamic period is also possible since the heraldic poses of the eagles and gryphons may suggest a workshop in western Iran, Syria or even Constantinople.

87a220a9-b576-558f-8ef5-a66e51fa7a04.name: *Hirz* (Necklace) with Qur’an case
87a220a9-b576-558f-8ef5-a66e51fa7a04.short_description:
This beautiful *hirz* (necklace) is a rare example of artistry from the 14th century AH/20th century AD which includes identification of the artisan. The inscription reads, "Made by Said bin Hamad bin Humaid al-Hajrion 26 Rabi" al-Awwal 1386 AH.  
  
It is a central belief of Ibadhi Muslims that work is done for the glory of God, not for the glory of self. This custom of humility before God persists today, with work signed for reasons of practicality rather than self-aggrandisement. Signatures are typically modest in terms of scale, placement and style of execution. It is not unusual for artisans to sign their work with the name of the town or *souq* (local market) where their workshop is located in lieu of a personal signature.

884d9ccd-97ec-51c8-aec6-d384ad59224c.name: A Tunisian decoration (on the right) and an Italian decoration (on the left) awarded to a member of the Moreno family
884d9ccd-97ec-51c8-aec6-d384ad59224c.short_description:
Two members of the Moreno family, Raffaello (Tunis 1844-1913) and his brother Leone (Tunis, 1852-1940) were awarded honours both by the Italian King (Cavaliere dell’Ordine della Corona d’Italia) and by the Bey of Tunis (Nichan Iftikhar). The Morenos were Jews from Livorno (Italy), who had migrated to Tunisia in the early 19th century.  
Other Italians migrants in Tunisia were awarded both the title of Cavaliere dell’Ordine della Corona d’Italia by the Italian King and the title of Nichan Iftikhar by the Bey of Tunis, including Giuseppe Di Vittorio (a Sicilian who ran a construction company) and Luigi Rey (born in Tunis to an immigrant family from a village north of Turin, Piedmont, Italy, who also ran a construction company) and the Jewish Doctor Giacomo Castelnuovo.

8dff808a-ff1a-5d4a-951e-f0b15fd77e9d.name: Septum Nose Ring
8dff808a-ff1a-5d4a-951e-f0b15fd77e9d.short_description:
This is a nose ring worn through the nasal septum, known as an *arawak* or *arabek*. Such nose rings serve as a marker of ethnic identity and marital status among elderly Arabic women in the settlement of Jeynau. According to Jeynau residents, this type of jewellery distinguishes them from other Central Asian ethnicities. The section of the ring that passes through the septum is made of flattened silver wire that forms a crescent shape, resembling a bow. One end of the septum section is left unattached, and this open end is inscribed with cuneiform carvings and notches. The other end of the septum section is soldered to a length of silver wire that forms the base of the ring. Rather than connecting to the open end of the septum section, the wire curves back upwards and twists around the septum section to form a loop. Within this loop of wire, beads decorate the ring. First, there is a large bead made of a cobalt-coloured semi-precious stone. In nose rings of this kind, the largest blue or green bead is called *latwa tash* (“the guarding stone”), as the nose ring is traditionally understood to be a guarding amulet. Working outwards from the *latwa tash*, there is also a spiral of silver wire, a smaller bead made of a coral-like stone, and another spiral of silver wire. Typically, the septum nose ring can be used to secure a face veil. Some Jeynau women instead wear a chain connecting their nose ring to their temple pendant as a symbolic replacement of the face veil; veils are not widespread in Bedouin communities.  
Arab settlers brought the tradition of the septum nose ring to Central Asia. Due to the Arab conquests, Arab tribes established settlements in northwest Arabia, along the Great Silk Road, and ultimately in the region now known as Uzbekistan by the 10th/16th century. These tribes can be traced back to modern-day Afghanistan, specifically the cities of Aghan Balkh, Shibarghan, and Andkhoy. A close parallel to Jeynau septum nose rings was recorded in the Dhofar Governorate (the Sultanate of Oman). The Dhofar septum nose ring is called a *khasafa* or *khasama*, and it indicated girls’ marital status; at puberty a girl's nasal septum was pierced for the nose ring she would wear once wed.

94a9dbbc-5b0a-5b70-8442-ce4c71510587.short_description: This beautiful finger ring, part of a group of objects from the al-Busaid Dynasty, is an excellent example of one of Oman's oldest design elements, a simple pattern formed from circles with central dots. This design has been dated to the 4th millennium BC. Later examples from the 3rd and 2nd millennium BCE show this design typically arranged in rows and combined with linear elements. Today, dot-in-circle patterns continue to be used by Omani artisans on the silver jewellery of northern Oman and on the pottery of Dhofar.

94bc6d72-5113-5a70-8c92-5cbd435c2e55.name: Rose-water flask
94bc6d72-5113-5a70-8c92-5cbd435c2e55.short_description:
The flask has a polyhedral body divided into a series of six lozenges with three pairs of pheasant-like birds and triangular half lozenges with scroll palmettes. The upper and lower sections of the neck and the shoulders have *kufic* inscriptions against a ring-matted background. Starting with the band around the top of the neck, they read: ‘For the Most Mighty owner, the Learned, the Just, the one helped \[by God\], the Victorious, the one Triumphant over the kingdom (*Nusrat al-Dawla*) and religion (*Nusrat al-Din*) may his glory be everlasting.’  
  
The parallels to Sasanian silver, and to the decoration of Sasanian and early Islamic textiles, are clear and suggest that the decorative repertoire of silver was markedly more conservative than of objects in base metal. The form also recurs in glass of a rather later date.

9b9b293c-0f7f-5225-8785-1a295c4c8c6a.name: Incense burner.
9b9b293c-0f7f-5225-8785-1a295c4c8c6a.description:
This spherically shaped incense burner has a very varied composition. The lid takes the form of a fretted dome, decorated with interlacing foliage elements and surmounted by an open rosette encrusted with coral. The lower half, in which the incense is placed, features the same ornamentation. The two halves are attached to one another via a hinge and a small chain, from which hangs a ball of coral. The entire piece rests on a round base at an angle, on gentle volutes encrusted in coral and decorated with stylised vegetal elements that alternate with damascened surfaces that stick out.  
The aromas of incense or of amber, burning inside on hot charcoal, escaped through the perforated lid.  
Used inside both homes and mosques during religious festivities, the incense burner contributed a pleasant aroma to the surrounding environment.

Squares, rectangles, diamonds and incremental components of triangles are all in widespread use as elements of Omani design. Simple patterns formed by straight, intersecting lines are most easily executed and therefore predominate on the hardest materials – stone, bone, metals and hardwood. In woodwork, angular designs are often faceted, a technique which enhances visual interest through the interplay of light and shadow.

9f677e6f-1913-5ba1-b196-5a3e7d1c4fc7.name: *Pontifical Ceremonial Jug and Basin*
9f677e6f-1913-5ba1-b196-5a3e7d1c4fc7.description:
This oval basin, incised on its perimeter, is decorated with a strip of wrought ornamentation with festoons, grids, roses and a pair of *putti* heads. Its perimeter features a half-figure of St. John of Nepomuk, the patron saint of the person who commissioned the work. Opposite is a wrought oval label with a winged column representing the emblem of the Nová Říše Abbey, and engraved initials of the person who commissioned the piece, *N.A /W./P.N./C.G.* (*Nobilis Abbas \[Johannes Nepomucenus\] Wyminko, Praepositus Neureuschensis /C.G.*). Provost Jan Nepomuk Wyminko/Vejminko (c. 1683–1755) graduated from Hradisko, near Olomouc. He was provost of the Premonstratensian Abbey in Nová Říše from 1725 to 1732; in 1733 he was appointed the monastery's first abbot.  
The jug and basin are part of a luxurious set that included ceremonial cruets and a chalice (not preserved). The works, both in their shape and decoration, are derived from Augsburg models (for example, those created by masters of the Biller and Drentwett families). The jug serves for purification at the mass: the priest uses it to wash his hands before taking the blood and body of the Lord. Any spilt water is caught in the basin.  
Josef František Rossmayer probably took his apprenticeship in Prague and after journeyman's service abroad was appointed master in Olomouc in 1730. He made, among other things, candlesticks “in the Augsburg manner” for the main altar of the Sv. Kopeček Church, near Olomouc, a chalice with enamel figures of Christ's relatives for Brno cathedral and bindings for missals for the cathedral in Olomouc, in which he combined Augsburg and French models known from prints.

a0806d9b-0bf1-52cf-8538-62ee4530485b.name: Bowl with floral arabesque
a0806d9b-0bf1-52cf-8538-62ee4530485b.short_description: This shallow bowl has a separate disc riveted to the centre. The ornamentation represents almost the entire repertory of mid-16th century Ottoman decoration. A split-leaf arabesque is engraved on the disc; the cavetto has interlaced quatrefoil medallions and cloud scrolls; on the outer walls the half medallions are engraved with saz and rosette design. Broken stems around the base recall the mannerism of the Sünnet Odası panels, the Rüstem Pasha tiles and ceramic dishes from circa 1545-50.
keywords: Arabesque; Saz design; Ottoman metalwork

a0be739f-bf67-5116-9ebd-ce73ca66626f.name: Magharif (Spoon)
a0be739f-bf67-5116-9ebd-ce73ca66626f.short_description:
The date palm tree (Phoenix dactylifera), an enduring symbol of Oman, is identified with the early oasis Civilisation of Magan in the 3rd millennium BC and the taming of the desert. It is one of the few tree species specifically mentioned in the Holy Qur’an, and according to Islamic tradition Maryam (Mary) gave birth to 'Iesa (Jesus) in the shade of a palm.  
  
Highly simplified palm motifs such as those adorning this *magharif* (spoon), reminders of the teachings of the Holy Qur'an, appear as principle design elements often combined with geometric or floral elements to create circular or linear patterns as a repetitive motif.
keywords: Magharif; Spoon; Date Palm; Holy Qur'an; Floral

a1b3f2ad-cd29-5ce6-94f0-ebd7a60fff72.name: Kohl holder
a1b3f2ad-cd29-5ce6-94f0-ebd7a60fff72.description: This kohl holder, from Bedouin communities of the Naqab Desert, dates to the early twentieth century and is an example of coin-adorned accessories from Palestine. a5b2fd9b-e8df-5b2a-b618-52f1601e4e7a.name: Powder container.
a5b2fd9b-e8df-5b2a-b618-52f1601e4e7a.description:
This very curved horn-shaped container is made of wood covered with red velvet. It was fitted with two rings that enabled it to be attached to a rider's neck or waist with a strap. The mouth, tip and centre are decorated with cylindrical and conical plaques in gilded, engraved silver openwork. Whether embroidered with gold thread on the velvet covering or engraved and rendered in openwork on the silver plaques, the decoration consists mainly of plant motifs: stems, foliage, palms and fleurons borrowed from the traditional artistic repertoire of Morocco and Andalusia. A single geometric element, an eight-pointed star that marks the centre of the central metal plaque, stands alone among the plant decoration.  
This type of container, whose curving shape is reminiscent of the Yemen *jambiya* dagger, contained the powder used to load the rifles used in the *fantasia* and was part of the equipment carried by the horsemen of the north of Morocco who took part in games on richly harnessed steeds.
a5b2fd9b-e8df-5b2a-b618-52f1601e4e7a.short_description: Powder horns of this type, whose shape is reminiscent of the curve of the Yemeni *jambia* dagger, carried the powder used to load the rifles used in *fantasias*. They were carried by the horsemen of Northern Morocco who participated in such games on sumptuously harnessed horses.

a610d51e-269b-57af-bb7c-ff15d5cae8f8.name: Pen box
a610d51e-269b-57af-bb7c-ff15d5cae8f8.short_description: Pen boxes with separate compartments for the *qalam* and all the other accessories were used all over the Islamic world. They were fashioned in numerous shapes, most of which are rectangular with either square or rounded ends. A different type is the East Iranian wedge shape, made in two parts, with an inner, compartmented box that could be entirely removed. These pen boxes were probably pushed through the belt, a fashion which was retained up until Ottoman times.

a65ae972-d872-5b79-975c-3a0ac79cc20b.name: *Shawkah* (Brooche)
a65ae972-d872-5b79-975c-3a0ac79cc20b.short_description: This *Shawkah* (Brooche) is a fine example of squares, rectangles and diamonds and their integral components as a prominent design motif in Omani jewellery. Simple patterns formed by straight, intersecting lines are most easily executed and therefore predominate on the hardest materials – stone, bone, metals and hardwood. In woodwork, angular designs are often faceted, a technique which enhances visual interest through the interplay of light and shadow. Angular patterns are also prevalent in weaving and basketry, where methods of construction dictate the use of linear elements.

a98d0e50-3029-5377-a2cf-b09ed33dce7b.name: *Hirz* (Necklace) with Qur’an case
a98d0e50-3029-5377-a2cf-b09ed33dce7b.short_description: The iconic *hirz* (necklace) with Qur’an case is imbued with religious significance, having as its central feature a rectangular or cylindrical box in which protective verses from the Noble Qur’an are kept. Qur’an cases may be simply strung on a silver chain or rope or featured as part of a much larger necklace as seen here with silver beads, coins and amuletic pendants. Smaller cases are also used as hair ornaments and incorporated in headdresses.

aa69e40a-8b6f-5533-b199-6d9e6bc16fba.name: *Ghazal* (Knife)
aa69e40a-8b6f-5533-b199-6d9e6bc16fba.short_description: The highest quality of these pocket knives have a blade made of steel and handle made of the core of a ghazal’s horns. The sheath is usually made of wood and decorated with silver plated leather. Arabesque patterns are used extensively in traditional Omani woodwork, plasterwork and metalwork as a means of covering entire surfaces or precise areas within a defined geometric framework. The symmetry of this design can be noted in this excellent example, a *ghazal* (knife) from the mid-20th century. The term, "Arabesque", can be defined in two ways within the context of Islamic design; as a specific decorative element consisting of a continuous branching stem with split palmate leaves, or in a larger sense, referring to an entire range of designs based on stylised floral, foliar and animal motifs. The aesthetics of the Arabesque are derived from the imposition of order on the natural world.
aa69e40a-8b6f-5533-b199-6d9e6bc16fba.dates: Mid 14th century AH / Mid 20th century AD

aaa3d2b6-39e1-57a0-8e51-58d7bf3405b2.name: Sword Hilt with Design of Lion Heads, Arabesque Scrollwork, and Arabic Inscription
aaa3d2b6-39e1-57a0-8e51-58d7bf3405b2.short_description: A gold sword hilt worked in repoussé and elaborately engraved with panels of scrollwork and a band of inscription highlighted with niello (a black metallic alloy of sulfur, copper, silver, and lead that was laid into the engraved area and heated to create the contrasting background). The inscription surrounds the blade opening. Lion heads adorn the quillions (the horizontal element of the handle which protects the hand). The handle and blade openings are surrounded by finely worked gold twisted rope rings. The handle socket is octagonal, its panels alternating between sides of overall-engraved scrollwork, with single delicate arabesque designs in the center. The cross-section of the handle socket is octagonal.

ad19784d-75e7-5769-a81f-2ceb7584b743.name: Book Cover
ad19784d-75e7-5769-a81f-2ceb7584b743.description:
A Baroque book cover of embossed silver and richly decorated with volutes, shells and acanthus foliage. Both the front and back covers have a central crest of two important families: the Crest of the Gaos (Gaus?) family of Rijeka on the front, and the crest of the Brajković family of Senj on the back. Mentioned initially in Rijeka in 1614, The Gaos (Gaus?) family appear in a document of 1616, as “de Hahnberg”. The Brajkovićs of Senj are a prominent Croatian family, descendants of the Miroslavić family, first mentioned in Poljica in 1420. One of the best-known members of the family was Martin Brajković (Senj 1668–Vienna 1708), Bishop of Senj and Modruš from 1700 to 1703, and Bishop of Zagreb from 1703 until his death in 1708. Who ordered this book cover and why is unknown; similarly how these two families are connected in the first half of 18th century is also an unknown.  
There are two silver hallmarks on the object: one is a Venetian hallmark with St. Marcus, and the other is the control mark of Venetian mint “Zecca” that belongs to Zuanne Premuda who worked at assay control from 1712 to 1749.

One of the best-known members of the Brajković family was Martin Brajković (1668–1708), Bishop of Senj and Modruš, and later Bishop of Zagreb.

af522df8-2bb6-5764-b5cf-7a2ae9be0f31.name: Kaaba Key
af522df8-2bb6-5764-b5cf-7a2ae9be0f31.short_description:
Silver-inlaid inscriptions embellish this bronze key attached to a moon-shaped ring. Its unique profile safeguards the house of God in Islam.  
  
The inscriptions bear religious and political messages, including Qur’anic verses and the name of Sultan Abd Al-Aziz, commissioner of this key in the 19th century.  
  
Prophet Ibrahim and his son Ismail are believed to have raised the sanctuary’s foundations, carrying a sacred tradition of guardianship. Today, the Shayba family preserves the key in a bag made of silk, gold and silver. As authorized keykeepers entrusted by Prophet Muhammad (PBUH), twice a year, they unlock the Kaaba for purification with rosewater and holy water.

b23d072c-13ac-5c66-9709-b4cefd84d692.name: Inkwell with Oriental decoration
b23d072c-13ac-5c66-9709-b4cefd84d692.short_description: The use of this type of inkwell was borrowed in the Romanian lands from the Ottomans. This particular inkwell belonged to Ion Ghica, one of the Romanian politicians who prepared the 1848 Wallachian revolution. As member of Wallachia’s revolutionary committee, he was sent to Istanbul before the start of the revolution to have talks with Ottoman officials and the ambassadors of European states, in an attempt to convince them to support the claims of the Romanian revolutionaries. After the revolution was defeated, he remained in Istanbul. Between 1854-1857 he was governor of Samos. In 1866, after the election of Carol of Hohenzollern as prince of the United Principalities, Ghica went to Istanbul (May-July) to try to obtain the recognition of his reign.

b269b5d1-fa64-52f1-83ee-615537fde662.name: Golden bowl of Altstetten
b269b5d1-fa64-52f1-83ee-615537fde662.description: In Zurich, gold is something one expects to find in and around the financial centre at Paradeplatz. So you can imagine the surprise of the man working on the rail tracks in Altstetten in 1906 when his eye caught sight of a glint of gold shimmering through the mud. What came to light was a richly decorated bowl. It turned out to be one the most significant Bronze Age finds. The precious bowl had been lying in the ground, well protected, for about 3,000 years. Suns, full moons and crescents decorate the bowl. The noble material’s bright gloss also represents the heavenly lights. Even back in the Bronze Age people made use of the celestial bodies to orient themselves and keep track of the course of the seasons. They were aware of the sun and moon’s influence on the growth of crops and relied on them as symbols in their rituals.
keywords: archaeology; golden bowl; Altstetten

b2951b28-6ec4-56f6-8f05-fa36ac2f0bef.name: Mirror
b2951b28-6ec4-56f6-8f05-fa36ac2f0bef.short_description: The silver facing of this mirror is a rare instant of precious metalwork to survive from the Fatimid era. It is decorated with typically Fatimid scrolls, heart-shaped motifs and benedictory *kufic* inscriptions. The mirror’s circular shape with a pierced central boss allowing a string to pass through and be used as a handle has its origins in China. The Chinese models may have reached Egypt either via Iran or by the Indian ocean and Red sea trade route.
keywords: Mirror; Kufic; China; Fatimid; Metalwork; calligraphy; inscription

b2ca91ca-c46b-5e08-b073-5f3ded54c993.name: Monstrance of the Bemposta
b2ca91ca-c46b-5e08-b073-5f3ded54c993.alternate_name: Monstrance of the Chapel of the Palace of Bemposta or Palace of the Queen
b2ca91ca-c46b-5e08-b073-5f3ded54c993.description:
This magnificent monstrance in gilded silver and gold with a triangular base, sits on three volutes ornamented with floral motifs, ribbons and cartouches. On the three inferior angles of the base there are cherubs and three figures that symbolise Faith, Hope and Charity. On the top corners there are three full-bodied angels conveying Eucharistic motifs, while six cherubs and seraphs, overlap, ascending along the stem.  
On the three faces of the base oval bas-reliefs represent themes from the Eucharist: The Supper at Emmaus and the giant bunch of grapes, Fruit from the Promised Land and Christ at Calvary.  
The monstrance' sunburst is encircled by clouds. It has a radiant splendor with irregular rays, covered with precious stones. The monstrance's surface is entirely adorned with precious stones, some of them large and of excellent quality, creating a spectacular decorative and chromatic effect.  
The theatrical splendor of the Baroque is well illustrated through the use of jewels and quality chiselling, admirably assembled in a dazzling combination of metal and gemstones.  
It is likely the monstrance was commissioned by King Pedro III, husband of Queen Maria I. In Pedro III's Will of 1786 he foresees that his son, the future King João VI, should have the country house in Queluz, and urges him to care for the divine cult traditionally associated with the Bemposta Chapel, where he wished the precious monstrance to be kept.  
Attribution of this piece is controversial. Traditionally, researchers attributed it to J. F. Ludovice, the goldsmith and architect of the Convent of Mafra. Their theories were based on an existing drawing of the monstrance at the Museum, which also came from the Bemposta Palace.
b2ca91ca-c46b-5e08-b073-5f3ded54c993.short_description: A majestic monstrance in gilded silver with precious stones that creates a spectacular chromatic effect. The theatrical splendor of the Baroque is well illustrated through the use of jewels and quality chiselling, admirably assembled in a dazzling combination of metals and gemstones.
b2ca91ca-c46b-5e08-b073-5f3ded54c993.method_for_datation: Vassalo e Silva (2000) proposed that Adão Gottlieb Pollet both designed and made the monstrance. This is based on a specific analysis of the application of the gemstones. Although initially the  monstrance was dated to 1740–1750 the date is now thought to be later, 1775–1780.

b2cb8a2c-1f55-57a0-adad-cfa00604a828.name: Bookcover
b2cb8a2c-1f55-57a0-adad-cfa00604a828.short_description: The all-over pattern adorning this gilded binding highlights the design and decoration of the central field. The busy central field displays at its centre a scalloped medallion and pendants filled with arabesque and *hatayi* scrolls, Chinese cloud scrolls, rosettes and leaves. Similar pattern decorates the corner-pieces. The main panel is surrounded by four L-shaped lobed cartouches that are decorated similarly decorated with vegetal scrolls. This all-over pattern is brushed over with gold paint – creating a shining surface. The common Persian "Lachak Toranj" (medallion and corner-pieces) design was developed in Persia for book covers and ornamental book illuminations in the 15th century, and it was integrated into carpet designs in the 10th/16th century. A similar motif can be found on two Persian carpets adorned with similar arrangement of medallion and corner-pieces with a symmetrical pattern occupying the centre of the field.

b2f01795-06d0-53f5-977b-6664d2f2de6b.name: *King João V of Portugal Drinking Coffee and Chocolate*
b2f01795-06d0-53f5-977b-6664d2f2de6b.description:
This interesting miniature, set within an ornate silver frame displaying the royal coat of arms, is one of only a few remaining objects from the Joanine court to have survived the Earthquake of 1755. According to the family of the Marquis of Foz, to whose collection this miniature belonged until 1901, this scene represents King João V being served drinking chocolate at home by the Duke of Lafões. However, in the corner of the miniature is the date 1720, making the Foz identification of the duke implausible given that the duke was born in 1718 and would have been two years old at the time this picture was painted. The most plausible hypothesis is that the person depicted is Prince Miguel of Braganza, the half-brother of the King and father of the future Duke of Lafões, who would, therefore, be the child represented. The Foz family also asserted that the Marquises of Angeja and Alegrete appear in the painting, as well as the painter himself and the house chaplain, however, firm identifications have been neither consistently contradicted nor confirmed.  
The objects depicted in this composition are noteworthy: the utensils associated with painting are in the foreground: a pallet, brushes and a sketch on a piece of paper. The objects related to drinking: a coffee pot, hot chocolate maker, tea cups and a bottle, alluding to the popularity of chocolate and coffee both of which became extremely fashionable among the Portuguese aristocracy and throughout the rest of Europe.  
Although the scene suggests a relaxed and jolly atmosphere, the strict etiquette and hierarchy of the Joanine court is present within the structure of the composition: the representational field is divided into two halves, with the higher ranking figures on the left-hand side.  
Nothing is known about the identity of the miniaturist, although his name suggests that he might be one of many Italian artists who, together with other foreigners, came to work in Portugal during the reign of João V. The frame presents plant-like decorations with acanthus, volutes and shell shapes in chiselled and embossed silver – a feature associated with the first quarter of the 1700s. The frame is surmounted by a shield and crowned with the Portuguese royal arms sustained by two lieutenant *putti.* A grotesque mask at the bottom centre is typical of this phase of the Baroque period. A chiselled frieze with laurel leaves serves as an internal frame for the miniature.

b65922f4-01d3-5457-a9bc-98f6df701f87.name: Gospel cover of Dorotheos Proios from Edirne
b65922f4-01d3-5457-a9bc-98f6df701f87.short_description: The gospel comes from Adrianople, but a handwritten note on the second page notes that: "…it was crafted and decorated here in Smyrna". From around the mid-eighteenth century Smyrna was the second most important port of the Ottoman Empire, and an important part of its economic life was in the hands of Greeks. The “Frankish quarter” and the preponderance of large-scale, foreign trade gave o cosmopolitan air to Smyrniot society. There is strong western European influence on this impressive silver cover made for Dorotheos Proios. Scrolled cartouches, thronging garlands of roses and conch shells in high relief make it a triumph of Rococo art, at least after the fashion in which it was understood in the Ottoman Empire. Smyrna was an important centre of silver production, but the designs were in general circulation and compositions were put together to fit the circumstances.
