b9d55563-3221-5150-9626-d1ff8d78bba0.name: Kohl Container
b9d55563-3221-5150-9626-d1ff8d78bba0.short_description: Cosmetic kits such as this one, comprised of a kohl container and kohl stick, were used by both women and men in many countries to apply eyeliner. The use of kohl was widespread in Egypt from the Pharaonic period onwards, made from burning the saffron plant and combining it with raw copper and lead. Kohl was used to beautify the eyes as well as to medically treat them.  This mid-20th century kohl container is a fine example of use of the predominant Arabesque pattern used in Islamic design.  The Arabesque as a specific decorative element consists of a continuous branching stem with split palmate leaves. The aesthetics of the Arabesque are derived from the imposition of order on the natural world. Arabesque patterns are used extensively in traditional Omani woodwork, plasterwork and metalwork as a means of covering entire surfaces or precise areas within a defined geometric framework.

bd7a3cd3-6bbf-5036-bebe-7fdc38ffd56d.name: Monstrance
bd7a3cd3-6bbf-5036-bebe-7fdc38ffd56d.description:
The monstrance is by the Graz goldsmith, Hans Georg Pfisterer. The shaped oval base has enamel medallions showing scenes from the Passion of Christ and continues into a knob, shaped like a Baroque vase, from which rises the top part of the monstrance of the so-called sun type. Bands and foliate ornaments completely cover it intertwined with filigree and jewels. The opening of the ostensory has a six-sided moulded frame made up of wavy and angled sides and surrounded by airy filigree ornamentation of entwined scrolls and jewels that form flowers. Above the ostensory is a richly decorated canopy under which God the Father, holding the globe, hovers in clouds. Above the canopy is the dove of the Holy Ghost. At the foot of the frame, two adoring angels kneel on narrow decorated bases. The bottom edge of the monstrance has a lambrequin motif from which pearls hang.  
Bishop Juraj Branjug of Zagreb acquired the monstrance. He was one of Croatia’s most active bishops in 18th-century in the field of religious art building a new palace in Zagreb and renovating and building many churches. He had his own woodcarving workshop at Kaptol whose master craftsmen made altarpieces and pulpits adorned with the bishop’s arms for many churches. He bought and donated first-class liturgical objects to the cathedral.

c644f172-5e30-55ce-9c9e-f557428c4c25.name: Hand of Fatima
c644f172-5e30-55ce-9c9e-f557428c4c25.short_description:
This object represents the "Hand of Fatima" also known as *Khamsa* (the Arabic word for "Five"), "Hand of Venus" or "Aphrodite". Jewish silversmiths in Morocco became known for casting and engraving pieces such as this one, used as a talismanic doorknob or jewellery pendant.  
  
Carthaginian excavations traced the open hand to ancient Egypt, whose variations appear across all faiths and time as a representation of God and believed to grant protection against ill will. In Islam, Fatima, the beloved daughter of Prophet Muhammed (PBUH) defends anyone regardless of faith against evil.  
  
The hand appears symmetrical with the five fingers indistinguishable, embodying the secret codes of the number five in Islam. The fingers allude to the five pillars of Islam, five daily prayers and five keys to the unseen. While silver casts additional amuletic power, the phoenix and salamanders symbolize life, rebirth and fertility.

c8cfe806-d0a6-52f3-8548-dbfaefacc927.name: *Khatim bu Fas* (Finger Ring) with Crescent Moon and Stars
c8cfe806-d0a6-52f3-8548-dbfaefacc927.short_description:
The sun, moon, stars and planets guided early Omani navigators across oceans and deserts, and the observation of celestial phenomena gave rise to the lunar calendar as a schedule around which to plan habitual activities. In Islam, astronomical observation signals the start of the Holy Month of Ramadan and the *Hajj* (pilgrimage season) and determines the timing of daily prayers.  
  
Omani artisans use celestial symbols as expressions of the Islamic faith and universal representations of the natural world. Crescent moons and stars are especially prevalent in jewellery, ceremonial weaponry and in all forms of architectural adornment. Sun and earth emblems and constellations are also occasionally seen.

cbb6bbe3-72b1-5d00-b8a3-fc74f38248d4.name: Sacramento Monstrance
cbb6bbe3-72b1-5d00-b8a3-fc74f38248d4.description:
An exceptional example of Baroque workmanship during the period of King João V, the Sacramento Monstrance – also called the *Anjo Custódia* “Angel Monstrance” – assumes the form of an Atlantis angel, a figure that is sometimes incorporated into the lower part of gilded wooden altarpieces. In this particular case the Atlantis angel appears free; instead of the usual representation as a pillar sustaining a globe the angel holds a radiant sun. Theatrical tension is undoubtedly achieved with the decoration of the piece itself, but the monstrance would have been surrounded by the gilded wood of the sacred space of the high altar and the aim would have been to increase the emotional and devotional fervour of the congregation and lead them to contemplate the divine light of truth and its beauty.  
Symbol of the Church Triumphant, the monstrance is a splendid composition of contrasting effects: dynamic lines and imposing shape – the result of which sees the elegant sculptural angel in polychrome and gilded wood – and the resplendence of silver, colour and glinting of both the enamel and glass.  
The kneeling angel holds a spherical, smooth and polished monstrance enveloped in a corona of silver rays. Surrounding the *luna* – the space where the host is kept and exhibited – are Eucharistic symbols enhanced by brightly coloured enamel work, and mounted over a circular base with eight ornamental silver-gilt cherubs. Vegetal motifs and coloured glass form flowers to complete the decoration. The monstrance presents a municipal contrast between the silver from Lisbon (L), in use since 1690, and the incomplete hallmark of an unidentified goldsmith from Lisbon, whose initials were LRP, and who was active between the end of the 17th century and the first half of the 18th century.
cbb6bbe3-72b1-5d00-b8a3-fc74f38248d4.short_description: Holding the solar sphere made out of silver – glowing with the true Word of God – the Atlantes angel is supposed to increase the emotional and devotional fervour of the congregation and lead them to contemplate the divine light of truth and its beauty. This piece was probably the highlight of the gilded wood high altar at Sacramento Convent in Lisbon.

cbb6bbe3-72b1-5d00-b8a3-fc74f38248d4.method_for_datation: This goldsmith’s hallmark first appeared in the early part of the decade of 1690 and continued to appear throughout the first decades of the 18th century. The technical and stylistic affinities of both the figure of the Atlantis angel and the polychrome allow the monstrance to be placed within the Baroque style during the reign of João V (1707–1750).
cbb6bbe3-72b1-5d00-b8a3-fc74f38248d4.obtention: The monstrance came originally from the Santíssimo Sacramento Convent in Alcântara, Lisbon. Founded in 1612, the convent belonged to the female branch of the Dominican order and was closed after the death of the last nun in 1897. The monstrance was transferred to Coimbra in 1914 where it became part of the gold and silverware collection of the National Museum of Machado de Castro.

cd9c5acc-6762-581c-8259-b6b3a0d9e694.name: Pair of Torchères
cd9c5acc-6762-581c-8259-b6b3a0d9e694.description:
These two grandiose torchères were ordered for the Chapel of Saint John the Baptist to be installed in São Roque church in Lisbon. With a triangular base, in gilt bronze, they form a pyramid held by titans. Above, a cornice developing into a dome is finished with Rocaille-inspired shells and a D. João V shield on each of the three surfaces of the torch holders. In niches below the dome, forming an oratory, the Doctors of the church are seated: St Jerome, St. Thomas Aquinas, Sr. Ambrose and St. Bonaventure, St. Augustine and St. Leo the Great. The hybrid ornamentation develops upwards in fluid volutes – wing, acroterion, cymatium – flowers in the shape of garlands, phytomorphic elements – rope, laurel and acanthus – and zoomorphic elements, as well as a variety of *putti* inspired by the Roman Baroque.  
They were conceived and produced by Giuseppe Gagliardi with the cooperation of the metalworker Fellice Schiffone, the carpenter Lucano Celladini, Agostino Ancidoni another metalworker, and Lorenzo Morelli a silversmith and founder. Following the death of Giuseppe Gagliardi minor finishing and the lamination were concluded by his son, Leonardo Gagliardi, who like his father was a master silversmith.

Designed and produced by Giuseppe Gagliardi, the metalworkers Fellice Schiffone and Agostino Ancidoni collaborated with him on the project. Lucano Celladini was the carpenter and Luciano Morelli was the silversmith and founder.

d2105247-15f5-56b4-9a41-1c51ab776885.name: Lamp
d2105247-15f5-56b4-9a41-1c51ab776885.short_description: The lamp has a rounded, pierced body covered in foliate scroll with acorns and ribbons that form interlocking circles. The tall, convex neck is decorated with large acanthus leaves with wind-blown tips. From the base hangs a tassel made up of chains attached to Ottoman coins. The three suspension chains are attached to cast caryatids in softly pleated drapery holding plinths on their heads. The influence of Neoclassicism is obvious in the shaping of the neck, which is reminiscent of a vase, and in the use of caryatids instead of the angels which usually decorate lamps. The acanthus, though another Neoclassical motif, is used here with the naturalism and movement characteristic of Venetian lamps of the previous century (cat. no. 71). The lip is stamped with a semi- obliterated *tugra*.

d3f8650a-4599-5d0e-a22f-cd44a5f3ea38.name: The Pietroasa Treasure
d3f8650a-4599-5d0e-a22f-cd44a5f3ea38.short_description: One of the most valuable gold treasures of Romania is the Pietroasa hoard, which consists of five golden vessels and seven golden pieces of jewelry with a total weight of 19 kg. Dating from the centuries 4-5 AD, the hoard is attributed to the Goths. It was discovered accidentally in April 1837 by two peasants who sold it to an Albanian contractor named Verussi. Knowing that all treasures found in the Romanian soil had to be handed in to the authorities, Verussi tried to hide the hoard and even smashed some of the items to make them smaller. Even though he was eventually caught by the police, from the initial 22 items of the hoard only 12 were recuperated. The Pietroasa treasure was first internationally exhibited in 1867 at the universal exposition in Paris, where it enjoyed a great success.

e07117dd-950e-5f5f-9ae1-7e9e6b78feb2.name: Monstrance of the Golden Sun of Moravia
e07117dd-950e-5f5f-9ae1-7e9e6b78feb2.description:
This vessel, used for carrying the Host – the embodiment of Christ's flesh – the presentation of which constitutes the spiritual climax of a mass, is one of the most precious specimens of the goldsmith's craft in Moravia. An oval incised base supports a vase-like *nodus* bearing a sunburst with an aperture lined with a cartouche, accentuated by a crest motif. The typically Baroque, intricately undulating ornamentation with faggoting encircles a case with a lunette, a crescent for holding the Host.  
The sun as the source of life, light and Divine truth lent its name to a whole group of “solar” monstrances contrasting with medieval monstrances which were spire-shaped with Gothic pinnacles.  
The decoration features certain older elements originally associated with objects now lost. The most interesting of them is an enamel label set into the back of the monstrance leg. It depicts St. Wenceslas on a Gothic throne – the emblem of the Olomouc Chapter – with the coats-of-arms of Emperor Ferdinand III (1637–1662), brother of Leopold I Vilém of Habsburg, Bishop of Olomouc and Archduke of Austria. The Gothic-style throne in the chapter emblem, supplemented with Dietrichstein wine-maker knives, possibly represents the actual “throne of St. Wenceslas” in the Olomouc cathedral, commissioned by Bishop František of Dietrichstein.  
The origin of the monstrance was once associated with Cardinal Wolfgang Hanibal of Schrattenbach, Bishop of Olomouc, who bequeathed a significant amount of money for its creation. In fact, the monstrance was commissioned by the Olomouc Chapter, headed by Dean Kašpar Florentin of Glandorf and Canon Jiří Jindrich Mayer of Mayerswald, who also commissioned a missal decorated with wrought silver (1733). In recognition of its high artistic value, the monstrance remained Chapter property even after an imperial decree issued after the Napoleonic wars ordered that all objects with precious stones be transferred to Vienna.
e07117dd-950e-5f5f-9ae1-7e9e6b78feb2.short_description: This vessel, for carrying the Host, the embodiment of Christ's flesh, is one of only a few gold monstrances in Europe. The typically baroque, intricately undulating ornamentation encircles a case with a lunette, the crescent for holding the Host. The sunburst symbolises the source of life, light and Divine truth.
e07117dd-950e-5f5f-9ae1-7e9e6b78feb2.method_for_datation: Marked with hallmarks, it is the only known work by a Brno goldsmith demonstrating close contacts between Brno and Olomouc, the two main centres of Moravia. Although goldsmiths of the same name were also active in Augsburg and Linz, their family ties have not yet been proven.
e07117dd-950e-5f5f-9ae1-7e9e6b78feb2.obtention: Following extensive restoration, the monstrance, from the treasury of the Cathedral of St. Wenceslas Olomouc, is exhibited at the Archdiocesan Museum, Olomouc.

e296b3c2-f867-5011-9976-324fcf013681.name: Hammam bowl
e296b3c2-f867-5011-9976-324fcf013681.short_description: This bowl by its size, materials and design probably served as a water dispenser in hammam, a traditional Ottoman bath. Similar semi-spherical parcel-gilt silver vessels decorated in repoussé technique are often attributed as production by Balkan artisans of the AD 16th–17th centuries. Some of them are defined as drinking (wine) bowls for ecclesiastical and secular use. The Ottomans began to conquer Balkans in the 14th century. Rich silver mines of the region and the silver making tradition of the late Byzantine Empire fostered the development of Ottoman silverware. There is a peculiar detail in the design of the Khanenko Museum’s bowl. In the centre of the vessel an openwork gilt rosette is mounted on a pin with 5 cast figurines of birds applied above it. The rosette rotates. This made historians suggest that the device (and the bowl itself) was perhaps intended for splashing the flowing water as a kind of entertainment during hammam bathing rituals. The Khanenko Museum possesses three bowls of this kind, slightly different in design.
e296b3c2-f867-5011-9976-324fcf013681.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis by A. Ivanov (examination, date, origin), A. Makarevych (examination, 2018 date, origin and type of object specified).

e3f48d7b-3bf0-5b73-ae59-24ec80351340.short_description: The Tantur is an example of cultural tradition developed inside the contaminations typical of the Mediterranean world. It is decorated with symbolic images of leaves, flowers and animals and it is engraved with the year of Egira, 1172. Its cylindrical shape is reminiscent of an *asherah*, one of the emblems of the Phoenician goddess of fertility Astarte (the Siriac Atargotis), often represented with cylindrical headgear. The origins in terms of scientific activity and conservation of Museo Nazionale Preistorico Etnografico "Luigi Pigorini" in Rome, can be traced back to the foundation in 1875 of the "Royal National Museum of Prehistory and Ethnography in Rome" within the buildings of the Roman College.

e7628812-bff0-56db-90f6-eba9949466d5.name: Pair of Bracelets with Chased Decoration
e7628812-bff0-56db-90f6-eba9949466d5.short_description: *Hujuls* (Bracelets) such as these from the al-Busaid Dynasty, sometimes worn as anklets, were worn in paired sets by women and children in Central and Northern Oman. Small stones sealed inside rattle with the movement of wearer. These are fine examples of one of Oman's oldest design elements, circles with central dots. Its use on shell jewellery has been dated to the 4th millennium BC. More complex dot-in-circle patterns are found on 3rd and 2nd millennium BC soft-stone vessels where they are typically arranged in rows and combined with linear elements. Today dot-in-circle patterns continue to be used by Omani artisans working in clay, wood, copper, silver and many other materials. They are seen on wooden drums, axe blades and knife scabbards of the Musandam Peninsula, on the silver jewellery of northern Oman and on the pottery of Dhofar.

ea93f27b-2ec2-5723-a1f1-65b29d221852.name: *Talahiq* (Gunpowder Horn)
ea93f27b-2ec2-5723-a1f1-65b29d221852.short_description:
Arabic is a poetic language with expressive power, and Omanis are known to be articulate and moving storytellers and poets. Arabic calligraphy, prized as a means of communication and adornment, gives form to literary expression within a visual context. The traditional art of verbal expression remains popular in Oman today, and master poets and storytellers are held in high esteem. Proverbs, whether recited or written, serve as a means of imparting wisdom and human truths based on common sense and often take the form of a metaphor or a poem. Sources of proverbs include the sayings of the Prophet Muhammed and other thinkers and theologians.  
  
This gunpowder horn, which comes from the period of Imam Said bin Ahmed al-Busai’idi (r. 1783-1810 AD), the 2nd ruler of the al-Busai’idi of Oman and the son of Imam Ahmed, founder of the al-Busai’idi Dynasty, was designed to fill the powder pan of a matchlock gun. The large decorative top was removable for filling the horn, and the gunpowder was released at the narrow end by operating the lever along the inner curve. The horn is made of silver, which has been layered with gold, and it is decorated with stamped and chased work suggesting that it belonged to a prominent person. An extract of a poem by al-Mutannabi, a renowned 10th century AD poet, is inscribed on the side of the horn:  
  
'If death is inevitable ... Then it is shameful to die a coward.'

f50ec732-f02a-5c81-8530-9953b2cc241a.name: Prayer Box with Cover
f50ec732-f02a-5c81-8530-9953b2cc241a.short_description:
This silver prayer box encompasses rich engravings suspended from a neck chain. In Iranian, Omani and Yemeni tradition, these types of necklaces treasure a secret wish.  
  
Rolled paper amulets would fulfil wishes, alleviate pain and defend against the evil eye. It remains uncertain whether people wear the prayers on their chest to be read or locked away forever.  
  
By holding or handling the box, a person enacts the power of the amulet for themselves, a loved one, or even against someone as a curse. Like engraved charms in modern jewellery, magical signs may cast a mystical aura, with Islamic phrases often written in reverse.

fcdf9f09-6ccb-53ef-8eb1-9593c8000973.name: Tureen with tray and spoon
fcdf9f09-6ccb-53ef-8eb1-9593c8000973.alternate_name: Count of Aveiras’ Tureen with tray and spoon
fcdf9f09-6ccb-53ef-8eb1-9593c8000973.description:
The import of luxury objects from France enshrines the Portuguese external relations on the XVIII century. The then wealthy and prosperous Kingdom of Portugal elected Paris as the main purveyor of “wonders”, precious fabrics, cabinetry or golden jewelry. King João V was instrumental in the process and the patronage offered to artists, namely the goldsmith Thomas Germain, was maintained by his son and successor, King. José I. Nobles and diplomats accompanied the royal preference and ordered an extraordinary array of French artworks to decorate their palaces and castles.  
The round tureen, more accurately called *pot-à-oille* style, was commissioned in Paris by the Count of Aveiras, D. Francisco da Silva Telo e Menezes. A product of the Charles Spire's workshop, was made circa 1752-3, one of an identical pair.  
It's a superb *rocaille* silver piece, profusely decorated with floral motifs, *rocaille* shells and spirals, also present in the circular tray's rim. The cover depicts a hunting scene.  
The shell shaped spoon is another perfect example of silver carving, with a branch-shaped shaft covered by spiraling foliage and ending in a richly chased bowl.
fcdf9f09-6ccb-53ef-8eb1-9593c8000973.short_description: Round tureen, with four supporting feet, profusely decorated with extremely ornate *rocaille* shell, spiral and floral motifs. The center bears the arms of the Aveiras family, which also appear on the circular tray supporting the tureen and on the large spoon.

fd7ea3bd-87be-5e84-a68b-74d44c3f3fc9.name: Tomb
fd7ea3bd-87be-5e84-a68b-74d44c3f3fc9.description:
The tomb, which is made of gilded silver shaped like a reliquary, holds a casket within which a figurine of Christ lies. Resting upon a trilateral base and supported on the backs of three ivory dragons, the tomb is decorated with embossed and chased foliate and *rocaille* ornaments and jewels. Enamel tablets hold within them scenes from the Life of Christ. From the base, a halo rises surrounded by a border of double rays. Attached to the base are allegorical figures of Faith, Hope and Love, flanked by St. Peter and St. Paul, and above them the figures of the Fathers of the Church Saints Augustine, Ambrose, Jerome and Gregory. The centre of the sunburst halo holds an enamelled painting of the Virgin and Child in a jewelled frame. It is decorated with foliate and *rocaille* ornaments, supported by two gilded angels. Above the frame is a splendid jewelled crown with a pendant pearl, flanked by two small ivory angels.  
Made in Augsburg and bought for the treasury with money bequeathed by Cardinal Juraj Haulik (the first Archbishop of Zagreb enthroned in 1853) a great patron of the arts and patriot whose ideas reflected the Enlightenment spirit.
